## The first tag with no known credential leak

Eight audit rounds of the redactor and the URL guard. Every defect closed below was found
by measurement or by planting a failure, and the numbers are from real runs rather than
estimates. Two of the round-eight sections describe defects that a fix in this same release
had introduced.

This is the most heavily audited state the library has been in, and that is a statement
about effort rather than a guarantee. The six tags before it all leak credentials and each
one looked fine when it was cut.

**The module is `GruxKit` in this release**, and `Grux` from 0.6.0 onward. If you are held
at 0.5.0 for any reason, keep `import GruxKit` until you bump.

## The path heuristic, which was the largest defect

A GitHub permalink came out as `https://github.[REDACTED:HIGH_ENTROPY].md`, and measuring it
found the defect was roughly two orders of magnitude larger than the bug report. **Across
814 real paths and URLs taken off a working machine, 357 were destroyed, 43.9%.**

The common cause is a `.` anywhere earlier in the string. `.` is outside the token
alphabet, so the entropy match begins after it, which defeats both existing path signals at
once. Any Swift build directory did it.

A third signal was added, based on content rather than shape: a path segment is a NAME if
it is four characters or more, letters plus at most a hyphen or an underscore, no digits,
and at least one vowel, with three such names forming a majority of at least four segments.
The floor of four segments is set by the AWS secret access key, whose two slashes leave
three segments, so the most valuable credential the generic pass is responsible for can
never reach the new rule at all.

**Measured on both sides, causally.** Real path mangling fell from 357 of 814 to 2, and the
project's own corpus from 41 of 9,323 to 40. Cost: 24.0 secrets newly spared per 400,000,
measured over ten seeds and 4,000,000 trials as 240 newly spared against zero newly caught,
individual seeds ranging 15 to 31.

**Why it survived seven rounds is worth more than the fix.** There was a test asserting on
a GitHub permalink and it passed, because its fixture used a single-letter owner and a
single-letter repository, which is exactly what drags the mean segment length under 10. The
fixture had been fitted to the implementation rather than to reality.

## The leading slash was most of the published leak rate

This project had published a bare 40-character leak rate of "about 1.2 to 1.3%" for several
rounds, and it was being read as a general weakness of the entropy rule. It was one hole.
The empty-leading-segment signal fired on ANY token beginning with `/`, and a random base64
secret begins with `/` one time in 64, which is 1.56%.

Requiring a real absolute path to have more than one component takes the rate from 1.295%
to 0.875% on identical inputs, and leaves the path corpus at 2 of 814 and the project
corpus at 40 of 9,323 exactly where they were. A third of the leak closed at no precision
cost at all.

## Two live bugs behind three documentation claims

- **A plus-addressed email address was destroyed.** `+` set the base64-padding flag, and
  that shortcut returned true before any other rule was consulted. The brake is that `+` is
  the base64 tell only in a base64 alphabet.
- **"Most specific wins" was false wherever a credential actually sits.** The pattern pass
  correctly wrote `[REDACTED:STRIPE_LIVE_SECRET]` and then the URL and flag passes matched
  that marker AS a value and overwrote it. Nothing leaked; the casualty was the audit trail,
  which is the only thing the tag is for.

Five further findings were tests that could not fail, including one whose branch had no
coverage at all: deleting the line left the whole suite green, and the compiler said so.

## The review found a leak the same round had just introduced

The base64 brake added to fix the plus-addressed email spared a whole class of real token.
The error was one character wide: the code tested `+` **or** `=`, and `=` is padding shared
by both alphabets, so it says nothing about which is in use. A base64url token with its
padding retained tripped a brake meant for something else. That is the ordinary shape of a
password-reset token, an email-verification token or a signed cookie.

**Verified independently of its own fixtures.** A reviewer that wrote none of this code
generated 208,675 realistic url-safe-base64-with-padding tokens and measured the leak count
fall from 75 to zero. Five fixtures passing says the examples were fixed; that says the
class was.

Worth recording precisely because the prose was right and the code was wrong. Checking the
code against its own documentation would have caught this; checking the documentation
against the code, which is the usual direction, would not have.

## The IPv6 special-purpose registry was 8 rows of 25

The IPv4 table had been registry-complete for several rounds. The IPv6 one classified 8 of
the 25 IANA rows and allowed the other 17. That was never a decision, it was an absence.

Three of the seventeen were genuine holes and they share a shape: RFC 7723, RFC 8155 and
RFC 9665 assign anycast addresses at `2001:1::1`, `2001:1::2` and `2001:1::3`, and anycast
means the nearest responder absorbs the packet. For all three that responder is
infrastructure on the local network. Teredo at `2001::/32` was the last prefix with
embedded-IPv4 semantics still undecoded.

**The prefix trap is why this is a row-by-row table.** Denying `2001::/23` closes five rows
in one line and also denies AMT at `2001:3::/32` and AS112-v6 at `2001:4:112::/48`, which
are globally reachable services carrying real traffic. `3fff::/20` was the same mistake
caught a second time, by measurement rather than by review.

## URLGuard, the audit surface, and the tag map

- **`illegal character in host` was tagged `URL_DENIED`.** That is the null-byte smuggling
  denial, the only signal this guard produces that implies deliberate intent. It now has
  its own tag, `HOST_SMUGGLING`, and a test pins the whole reason-to-tag table.
- **A denylist entry written any of four ordinary ways blocked nothing at all.**
  `https://evil.com`, `evil.com:443`, `evil.com/path` and `*.evil.com` all silently matched
  no host while looking completely correct in a config file.
- **`http://evil.com../` walked past the denylist**, because one side of the comparison
  stripped one trailing dot and the other stripped all of them.
- **The attacker chose the audit label.** The bad-scheme reason interpolates the attacker's
  own scheme into itself, so `denylist://x` reported as `USER_DENYLIST`.
- **An indented PEM leaked its body verbatim**, and the fence neutralised one tag in one
  case.

**No SSRF bypass was found in the probing pass.** Thirty URL spellings were driven through
`evaluate`, including backslash-before-userinfo, circled digits, the ideographic full stop,
a percent-encoded IPv6 zone id and Alibaba's CGNAT metadata address. All thirty were denied.

## Full record

The complete narrative, including every wrong first attempt and the plants that confirmed
red was reachable, is in
[CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/dotcomjack/grux/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).

## Upgrade

0.6.0 renames the module and 0.6.1 raises the platform floor to macOS 14 and adds two
provider patterns. Current is:

```swift
.package(url: "https://github.com/dotcomjack/grux.git", from: "0.6.1")
.product(name: "Grux", package: "grux")
```
